extracted.intended_audience: federal trial judges and patent litigators preparing jury instructions and verdict forms
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and sample verdict form for patent litigation (AIPLA 2012), covering definitions, infringement and invalidity standards, damages, and guidance on presenting factual issues to a jury. Intended to be customized to a particular case's facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement damages requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover damages for contributory infringement, patent holder must either prove that the accused product necessarily infringes the patent in suit or prove acts of direct infringement by others to which accused infringer made a substantial contribution. Because damages for contributory infringement are limited by the number of instances of direct infringement, the patent holder must further prove the number of direct acts of infringement of the patent in suit (for example, either by showing individual acts of direct infringement or by showing that a particular class of products/uses directly infringes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: Dynacore Holdings Corp. v. U.S. Philips Corp., 363 F.3d 1263 (Fed. Cir. 2004); Cardiac Pacemakers, Inc. v. St. Jude Med., Inc., 576 F.3d 1348 (Fed. Cir. 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief summary of the technical disclosure in a patent to enable the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office and the public to determine quickly the nature and gist of the technical disclosure in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent applicant’s change to one or more claims or to the specification either in response to an office action taken by a Patent Examiner or independently by the patent applicant during the patent application examination process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation in which a claimed invention describes an earlier invention and, therefore, is not considered new and is not entitled to be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transfer of patent rights to another called an 'assignee' who upon transfer becomes the owner of the rights assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way the inventor actually knew to make or use the invention at the time of the patent application. If the applicant had a best mode as of the time the application was first filed, it must be set forth in the patent specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim of a patent is a concise, formal definition of an invention and appears at the end of the specification in a separately numbered paragraph. In concept, a patent claim marks the boundaries of the patent ... Claims may be independent or dependent. An independent claim stands alone. A dependent claim does not stand alone and refers to one or more other claims, incorporating whatever the other referenced claim or claims say.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete mental part of the inventive act which must be capable of proof, as by drawings, disclosure to another, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation Application (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed during the examination process of an earlier application which has the same disclosure as the original application and does not include anything which would constitute new matter if inserted in the original application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-In-Part (C-I-P) Application (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed during the application process of an earlier application which repeats some or all of the earlier application and adds matter not disclosed in the earlier application to support the addition of new patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations of the claimed invention contained in a patent application and issued patent, usually including several figures illustrating various aspects of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The required parts of a device or the required steps of a method. A device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every requirement of a patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A product or method that contains the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A description of the invention that is sufficient to enable persons skilled in the field of the invention to make and use the invention. The specification of the patent must contain such an enabling description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office whereby a Patent Examiner reviews the filed patent application to determine if the claimed invention is patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Date (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Date a patent application, with all the required sections, has been submitted to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of a patent occurring when someone makes, uses or sells a patented invention, without permission of the patent holder, within the United States during the term of the patent. Infringement may be direct, by inducement, or contributory. Direct infringement is making, using or selling the patented invention without permission. Inducing infringement is intentionally causing another to directly infringe a patent. Contributory infringement is offering to sell or selling an item that is an important component of the invention, so that the buyer directly infringes the patent. To be a contributory infringer one must know that the part being offered or sold is designed specifically for infringing the patented invention and is not a common component suitable for non-infringing uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation / Requirement (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A required part of an invention set forth in a patent claim. The word 'limitation' is often used interchangeably with the word 'requirement.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the requirements for securing a patent. To be valid, the subject matter of the invention must not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the time of the earlier of the filing date of the patent application or the date of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written communication from the Patent Examiner to the patent applicant in the course of the application examination process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is an exclusive right granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to an inventor to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, or selling an invention within the United States, or from importing it into the United States, during the term of the patent. The patent has three parts: a specification, drawings and claims. The patent is granted after examination of a patent application and the examination record is called the prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative branch of the U.S. Department of Commerce charged with overseeing and implementing the federal laws of patents and trademarks; responsible for examining all patent applications and issuing all patents in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously known subject matter in the field of a claimed invention for which a patent is being sought; includes issued patents, publications, and knowledge deemed publicly available such as trade skills and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution History (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete written record of the proceedings in the PTO from the initial application to the issued patent, including office actions and amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reads On (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim 'reads on' a device or method when each required part (requirement) of the claim is found in the device or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention is 'reduced to practice' when it is sufficiently developed to show that it would work for its intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process in which a patent is reexamined by the PTO to determine whether one or more claims are patentable with respect to submitted prior art (prior patents or printed publications). 'Ex parte' reexamination is initiated by the patent holder or a third party but does not include further participation by any third party. 'Inter partes' reexamination is initiated by a third party who continues to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A payment made to the owner of a patent by a non-owner in exchange for rights to make, use or sell the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (glossary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent; it is a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not that every requirement of claim 1 of its patent is included in Alleged Infringer’s accused product?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If yes, proceed to damages questions; if no, consider doctrine of equivalents or other defenses. Jury answers must be unanimous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under the Doctrine of Equivalents (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not that the accused product includes parts that are identical or equivalent to every requirement of claim 1 of Patent Holder's patent? For any requirement not literally found, does the accused product have an equivalent part to that requirement?

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement (jury elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not: (i) that Direct Infringer infringed claim 1; (ii) that Alleged Infringer supplied an important component of the infringing part of the product; (iii) that the component was not a common component suitable for non-infringing use; and (iv) that Alleged Infringer supplied the component with knowledge of the patent and knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing manner?

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing Infringement (jury elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Patent Holder proven that it is more likely than not: (i) that Direct Infringer infringed claim 1; (ii) that Alleged Infringer took action that actually induced that infringement by Direct Infringer; and (iii) that Alleged Infringer was aware of the patent and believed that its actions would encourage infringement of a valid patent, or alternatively that it was willfully blind as to whether its actions would encourage infringement of the patent?

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement (objective and subjective prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: 5a. Has the Patent Holder proven that it is highly probable that from an objective point of view the defenses put forth by Alleged Infringer failed to raise any substantial question with regard to infringement, validity or enforceability of the patent claim? If yes, then 5b. Has the Patent Holder proven that it is highly probable that the Alleged Infringer actually knew, or it was so obvious that Alleged Infringer should have known, that its actions constituted infringement of a valid and enforceable patent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 5a is 'no', jury skips 5b. The standard in 5a is an objective assessment; 5b addresses the actor's actual knowledge or willful blindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that the specification of the Patent Holder’s patent does not contain an adequate written description of the claimed invention?

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that the specification of the Patent Holder’s patent does not contain a description of the claimed invention that is sufficiently full and clear to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the invention?

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that the patent does not disclose what the inventor believed was the best way to carry out the claimed invention at the time the patent application was filed?

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (jury question and checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that claim 1 was 'anticipated' (i.e., not new)? If yes, check applicable reasons such as prior public knowledge/use in the U.S. before conception, patented or printed publication anywhere before conception, made by someone else in the U.S. before conception and not abandoned/kept secret, described in another issued U.S. patent or published U.S. application based on an earlier application, or named inventor learned of the claimed invention from someone else/was not first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide only the specific factual disputes to the jury; the verdict form should list only reasons applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Bar (jury question and checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that claim 1 was not filed within the time required by law? If yes, check reasons such as: claimed invention patented or described in a printed publication anywhere at least one year before the U.S. filing date; invention openly used in the U.S. at least one year before filing and not primarily experimental under the inventor's control; device/method using claimed invention sold/offered for sale in U.S. and ready for patenting at least one year before filing and not primarily experimental; patent holder had already obtained a foreign patent filed at least one year before the U.S. application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (Graham factors and jury role alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury may be asked to answer preliminary factual questions to assist the court on obviousness: (a) level of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention; (b) scope and content of the prior art; (c) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (d) secondary considerations/factors indicating nonobviousness (commercial success, long-felt need, unsuccessful attempts by others, copying, unexpected/superior results, acceptance by others/licensing, independent invention by others, other factors). Two alternatives are provided: (1) jury decides only the underlying factual issues and the court makes the ultimate legal conclusion on obviousness; or (2) jury answers the factual issues and may give an advisory verdict on the ultimate question of obviousness (but the ultimate judgment is a legal determination for the court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verdict form should require jury's findings on each factual issue so the trial judge may make the final determination; only the disputed factual matters should be presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship (jury question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has Alleged Infringer proven that it is highly probable that Patent Holder’s patent fails to meet the requirement to name all actual inventors and only the actual inventors?

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages – Lost Profits (verdict question)
rubrics_metrics.description: What lost profits, if any, did Patent Holder show it more likely than not suffered as a result of sales that it would with reasonable probability have made but for Alleged Infringer’s infringement? (jury to specify dollar amount)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If infringement found and invalidity defenses rejected, proceed to lost-profits and reasonable royalty questions; otherwise do not answer damages questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages – Reasonable Royalty (verdict question)
rubrics_metrics.description: For infringing sales for which Patent Holder has not proved entitlement to lost profits, what has it proved it is entitled to as a reasonable royalty: (a) on-going royalty payment of $[per unit] or % of total sales; or (b) one-time payment of $[amount] for the life of the patent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may specify ongoing or one-time payment; reasonable royalty may be determined using the hypothetical negotiation framework (see instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation/Statutory Bar Specific Reason Checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: When finding anticipation or statutory bar, verdict form contains checklists of specific factual bases to be checked (e.g., prior public knowledge/use, printed publication, on-sale, foreign filing more than one year earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only list and submit to the jury those specific factual questions that are in dispute to avoid superfluous instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations as Evidence of Nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may indicate nonobviousness include commercial success due to merits of the claimed invention; a long-felt need for the solution; unsuccessful attempts by others; copying of the claimed invention by others; unexpected and superior results; acceptance by others shown by praise or licensing; independent invention by others about the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verdict form should list only those secondary-consideration factors for which a prima facie showing has been made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict Form Design Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The sample verdict form is provided for guidance. It requires jurors to make specific factual findings underlying affirmative defenses (e.g., anticipation, statutory bars, obviousness). It is recommended that the verdict form present factual questions as specifically as possible and require jury findings on each factual issue so the judge may decide the ultimate legal questions (e.g., obviousness). The use of bracketed 'find and replace' terms facilitates tailoring to case-specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid submitting superfluous instructions; simplify tasks for court and jury; tailor the form to the particular factual disputes between the parties. The ultimate legal determination (e.g., obviousness) is for the court, even if the jury provides an advisory verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits Framework references (Panduit factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits are determined under the 'but-for' test and using Panduit factors (demand, acceptable non-infringing substitutes, market share, capacity, amount of profit, price erosion, cost escalation, collateral sales, doubts resolved against infringer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panduit factors are used to evaluate entitlement to lost profits; their subcomponents (demand, substitutes, capacity, etc.) should be evaluated as relevant to the case.
